synthesis:
## QE ArXiv Watch Weekly — Week ending Aug 17, 2026 (4 papers)

If you’re monitoring anything “smart” with ML scores—defect probabilities, anomaly logits, risk scores—this week’s hook is simple: **treat the model output like a process variable, but don’t pretend your Phase I data are i.i.d.** Kang et al. bake that reality into a vision-SPC framework with a bootstrap that *resamples images and augments them* to hit a target ARL. It’s a very “2026” answer to the awkward question we all face: *how do I set control limits when my statistic is coming from a deep net and the distribution is a moving target?*

### Vision + SPC that actually looks deployable
Kang et al.’s MODERN framework is essentially three parts you can imagine putting on a line tomorrow:

1) **MODERN-Net** outputs a per-image defect likelihood.  
2) **MODERN-Chart** is a one-sided EWMA-ish chart with a restart-at-zero mechanism to catch persistent upward drift (so you don’t “bank” old evidence forever).  
3) **MODERN-Diagnosis** repurposes the net to localize defects as ellipses (a pragmatic middle ground between “classification only” and full segmentation).

The practical nugget is the **Augmented Bootstrap** for control limits: resample in-control images *and* apply rotations/flips to mimic nuisance variation, then choose limits to hit ARL0 (e.g., 1000 on DAGM with limit 0.0275). On benchmarks they report very “on-the-change-point” behavior (Prop.On often 0.94–1.00) and ARL1 around 21 when the shift happens at t=21. The near-zero sdARL1 they report in places is… eye-catching; if you try this idea, you’ll want to sanity-check with more replicates and with augmentation sets that reflect your real physics (lighting, pose, blur), not just flips.

Also worth stealing: a **transfer monitoring** idea—reuse a pretrained network in a new setting only after an applicability check (they use a two-sample t-test). That’s not the final word on domain shift, but it’s a concrete gate you can operationalize.

### DOE, but with a “geometry” lens (and a cautionary tale about balancing)
Two DOE papers hit very different worlds, but they rhyme: **design should follow identifiability, not tradition.**

Liu et al. tackle multimodal neutron scattering for quantum magnets, but the method is the transferable part: they learn fast differentiable surrogates (implicit neural representations) and then compute an **observation-induced geometry**—a pullback metric from spectral derivatives—to tell you which parameter directions are stiff vs. sloppy. Imagine having a dashboard that says, “this experiment can’t possibly identify *that* parameter, no matter how much data you collect.” Their “sloppiness scores” line up with posterior uncertainty, and they use posterior predictive variance to pick the next measurement setting (rotation angle ψ). Net effect: faster convergence than fixed/sequential acquisition, and a clear story on why powder data under-identifies compared to single-crystal.

Hull et al. bring the same “stop doing things by habit” energy to randomized experiments with **bounded outcomes** (binary is the obvious case). Under a minimax worst-case MSE criterion, **independent Bernoulli(0.5) assignment is optimal**, and—here’s the twist—**balanced complete randomization is strictly suboptimal**. Even more provocative: paired randomization with pair fixed effects can be *twice* as bad in worst case. The recommended affine estimator is basically “center outcomes at the midpoint of the support and regress on centered treatment with no intercept” (a centered Horvitz–Thompson/OLS variant). If you run A/B tests on defect/no-defect, pass/fail, or any bounded KPI, this is a reminder that “always balance” is not a universal optimum—it depends on the loss you’re optimizing.

### Reliability angle: measuring bias in LLMs like we measure leakage in systems
X et al. deliver a clean reliability-style lesson for AI governance: **latent association is not a reliable predictor of behavioral leakage.** Across eight model/provider cells, they find strong “elite surname → high status” associations in probes, but decision-task leakage is usually practically small and often equivalent within ±0.10 SD. Correlations between association strength and decision leakage are basically noise (r ≈ 0.20 across models; ≈ 0.07 across cells). If you’re building audits, the takeaway is methodological: **treat “association” and “action” as different failure modes with different tests**, the way we separate component degradation metrics from system-level hazard.

### The question to take into next week
As more of our monitoring statistics become ML outputs, are we ready to standardize “Phase I for models”—control limit setting, domain-shift gates, and diagnostics—so it’s as routine as an X̄-R chart? Or are we still pretending the score stream is just another sensor?
